Jewish confirmation. This ceremony reaffirms religious commitment and Jewish identity, typically held in Reform and Conservative synagogues for adolescents around age fifteen to sixteen. Unlike bar and bat mitzvah, which marks the onset of religious obligation, confirmation emphasizes personal choice and commitment to Jewish life and values. It is often celebrated on or near Shavuot, the festival that commemorates the giving of the Torah at Mount Sinai.

Confirmation emerged in nineteenth-century Reform Judaism as a way to mark maturing religious understanding, distinct from the bar and bat mitzvah. The timing on or near Shavuot is symbolic because Shavuot celebrates the Torah's gift to the Jewish people, and confirmands have often spent years in intensive Jewish education demonstrating their knowledge of Torah, Jewish history, and ethical values.

The ceremony itself involves formal, often solemn ritual. The celebrants wear special white or formal clothing and process to the bimah, the pulpit, where they recite vows or affirmations of Jewish commitment. A group ceremony is common, with multiple young people confirmed together, which emphasizes communal identity and shared values. This differs from bar and bat mitzvah, which can be individual celebrations.

The confirmation allows young people to articulate their own relationship with Judaism rather than marking an obligation that comes automatically at puberty. In some congregations, confirmands lead portions of the service, read from the Torah, or deliver speeches reflecting on their faith journey. This active participation demonstrates their deepening understanding and personal commitment.

After the service, a festive reception and celebration honor the confirmands' spiritual maturation and commitment. The young people are recognized not just as those who have reached a certain age, but as individuals who have chosen to affirm and deepen their place within the Jewish community.
